b:
Over the weekend, I spent a day and a half at 18North, a small, 18xx-themed “playcon” in St. Paul, Minnesota. Some of the folks I’ve gotten to know through Railways of the Lost Atlas—Kevin Delger and Jacob Schacht—are local to the Twin Cities area. I won’t claim to be a train game expert or a hardcore train game junkie, but I do enjoy private company auctions, track upgrades, route optimization, and the occasional financial shenanigan or two.
Normally when I hit tabletop shows, the shows are massive, shows like Gen Con, Festival International des Jeux, and SPIEL Essen. After spending a week in Germany at a show that hit 230,000 attendees last month, I was pretty excited about hitting a show that was a little smaller.
Maybe a LOT smaller.
18North was set to host about 50 people, tiny by SPIEL Essen standards. Sold!

18North is my second train game convention, after hitting TraXX in 2024. Like 18North, TraXX is a 50-ish person convention that takes place in a small conference room every year. Both cons have a library of train game titles that are the absolute opposite of the word sexy. (Edu Valls was NOT hired for character illustrations for the game 1817. In part, that’s because there are no character illustrations in 1817!)
Many of these 18xx titles are in simple, white cardboard boxes in print-and-play formats, with cover artwork featuring a train blowing its way through the American plains or the European wilderness. In some cases, you get historical photographs of people staring at a locomotive, as if a spaceship just landed on their front lawn.
This is part of the charm of these games; no one bothered to make most of the older 18xx productions attractive for people passing by a table at a coffee shop. It can serve as culture shock when games like the upcoming production of The Old Prince 1871 hit crowdfunding, because it’s almost impossible to believe that someone might bother to create something that looks more inviting than the front cover of a dry Hallmark anniversary card. (Sidebar: I love the TOP artwork. New ideas that move the 18xx production format forward? Count me in!)

Small conventions like 18North and TraXX end up being really magical to me, because they are often a person’s only chance in the course of a year to play the games that they really want to play en masse, with other enthusiasts who fit the profile of “a niche of a niche.” In the leadup to 18North, my 10-year-old kept asking when I would be flying to St. Paul to attend, using his running acronym, the “BTGC.”
BTGC stands for “Boring Train Game Convention.” (My kids like making fun of train games.)
Showing up at a small tabletop convention always has the look, the feel, the smell, the vibe of a room full of nerds…geeks, even. I arrived on the second day of 18North, replete with my 18North swag: 18North t-shirt, underneath a grey 18North no-zip hoodie. Of course, I’m a nerd, so I had some of my other train game gear in the travel bag: train t-shirt from my trip to Silverton, Colorado, striped train conductor cap, green TraXX t-shirt. Sadly, I forgot my train socks, a door prize from the TraXX show.

I had to have the gear to match the venue, because the geek stakes were high: 18North is hosted at an actual train depot, the Union Depot in downtown St. Paul. I mean, can you imagine? A train game convention, INSIDE A TRAIN STATION? A train station featuring a hobby train store in the lobby? If any of you know of something more geek than a train game convention inside of a train station, please list this in the comments…with some level of certainty, I will come to your convention in 2027.
The actual 18North play area is contained within a small conference room on the second floor of the depot, with a nearby breezeway that leads to an overlook where you can see the main seating area of the station.

Union Depot adds flavor to the whole affair, but ultimately, 18North is the kind of “BTGC” that reminds me of what I love about all small shows like this…it’s fun to play board games all day, even if I personally never do it. Other “tinycons” I’ve attended over the years inspired this article, such as the four-person weekend gaming event I did with three of my high school friends, to my Wednesday group’s annual “Lakecon” activity (about 10 people), to “Johncon” (my friend John’s birthday gaming event in Chicago, with in-and-out traffic that ranges up to about 15 people).
I don’t make much time for all-weekend gaming very often…in fact, 18North’s first day will end up being the only day I play board games from sun up to sun down for the entire year, because I’m sure I won’t have the time to do it again. But each time I commit, I love the result.

You’re probably wondering about the games I tabled across my ~18 hours at 18North. No, that amount of time was not intentional; work travel forced me to miss the first day of the show. Those jobs will get ya!
I did four plays at 18North: Shikoku 1889, 18Korea, 18Ireland, and Railways of the Lost Atlas with the recent expansion, Landmarks of the Lost Atlas. The games were mostly a good time, and as usual, that was thanks to the people. (Like most of these playcons, I showed up alone, not really knowing anyone besides the show organizers. Time to make some new friends!)
Prior to sitting down for my first game, I picked up my badge—18North organizer extraordinaire Phil Chen deserves a Lifetime Achievement Award for the level of organization he puts into something so intimate—and sorted through a list of what games were in the library, as well as which games other players had on their personal hit list. Phil’s badging system listed everything players needed to know: the four 18xx titles that player most desired to table during the show, their 18xx.games handle, their Discord name, their home town. (Something tells me Phil has run a networking event before.)

My play of Shikoku 1889 (or just “89”, because train gamers can’t be bothered to say the word “eighteen”) was a five-player game that kicked off my 9 AM start on Friday morning. A guy named Tucker and another person named Dan were sitting nearby; Tucker was looking to kick something off, and he had a hard stop at 1 PM to teach a scheduled play of 1833NE.
I introduced myself and stated my intentions: I was happy to play anything for the first game of the day. Tucker grabbed 89 and began to set up the game…two other folks who were local to Minneapolis, Aaron and Ben, walked in looking for two seats, so we collectively kicked off one of the fastest plays of 89 I’ve ever done in person. After setting up, our play only took about two hours, and we used a spreadsheet to math out the winner well before noon. (Tucker had an iPad ready to roll for the “spreadsheeting.” Train gamers, babeeee!)
The play was fun—89 is a classic for a reason—but the beauty of any small show is spending a little time with almost every single person at the event, especially if you are in town for a full four days and mix up your play groups. In case you haven’t heard, 18xx games are typically long, so while someone else is operating a company, it’s easy to squeeze in some small talk. Or talk a little smack. Or discuss the high points of maple-iced donuts from Dunkin. Or discuss their favorite non-train board games.

By the time we wrapped 89, the day was off and running…in the process, I made a couple more show buddies. Dan joined me for the Korea play. We picked up another player along the way: a guy named Dave, in town from California. That formed our threesome for Korea (and, like me, Dave arrived solo and was open to playing games with anyone else who showed up).
Korea was on my hitlist because of the current crowdfunding campaign for the “Big Box” edition; my only previous Korea play took place at TraXX, but I remember really loving the way the game’s player powers (Asset cards) and Korean War event changed up the typical 18xx formula. Our play at 18North this weekend turned Korea into a must-back.

We all loved Korea, but when you spend four hours playing a board game with other folks, you better find a way to enjoy it. Tiny playcons offer such a luxury when it comes to time; the brackets aligned with weeknight play were off the table, and we spent just the right amount of time re-reading parts of the rules that set Korea apart from other 18xx titles before setting the game up and diving in.
Turns took a while, but that didn’t matter to us. We had the kind of “competitive teamwork” I love when players are friendly and spending time getting to know each other. If Dan ran a route that didn’t take advantage of enough cash, I made sure to call out a more profitable route. When Dave ran a company that included Dan or I as a shareholder, he reminded everyone to grab chips from the bank. When I ran into the East Sea post-war, Dan made sure I got my $20 (whoops! ₩20!) bonus.

By the end of that four-hour opus, we used Korea to springboard into a much-needed dinner. Phil and Jacob joined us, and we walked into the Union Depot lobby for dinner at the Depot’s signature restaurant, 1881. (Friends, I wish I was kidding: the restaurant we hit at 18North, for an 18xx convention, in a train station lobby, is called 1881. Sometimes, the articles write themselves.)
After dinner, the five of us did Ireland, which was on Dan’s list and was a favorite of both Jacob and Phil. (In the end, it was NOT a favorite of mine, although I am told Ireland is better at a lower player count. I’ll never know.)
The gameplay itself was not a highlight, but the experience was, and our fivesome laughed a whole heck of a lot across a play that started at 7 PM and ran until the end of my night around 11. By the end, Jacob and I committed to a morning play of Railways of the Lost Atlas (“ROTLA”) with the expansion, so I hustled back to the local Springhill Suites for just enough sleep to get my brain ready for more math in the morning.

My final play of the weekend was so-so—Kevin and Jacob joined me and a fourth player, Chris, who was completely new to 18xx and made ROTLA and its expansion (complete with events, “direct-to-majors”, special tiles and the Metropolitan) his 18xx debut experience. To call this a tricky and unconventional introduction to a gaming system would be an understatement, so a HUGE kudos to Chris for jumping into the deep end.
I was out of play early—the other players cratered the value of my first minor, then I made a mistake calculating the number of 3 and 4 trains on the roster—but I love ROTLA’s variable map system and the elements that affect play because of each minor’s ongoing power. (This is not surprising, as a fan of Eurogames where players have a unique way to attack a game’s base systems.) All of us enjoyed helping Chris navigate some of the unique things about ROTLA in comparison to other 18xx titles Chris had studied, and sitting at the table with the same people for four hours created lots of chances to poke at the game decisions made during play.
After exchanging pleasantries, I got a picture with the group and made my way to the airport. I thought a lot about 18North and my desire to spend a couple more days next year playing games all day.
I know I’m lucky; I usually play games every day when I’m in Chicago, either with my groups or with my family, for at least a few minutes, sometimes much more. Settling in for a long day of games, at a small convention in environments where it is easy to meet new players, is a must…now it is on me to find a way to make that happen a little more often!
